# A GLM Conditional on Latent Group Effects

Generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) combine two ideas: a generalized linear
model for a non-Gaussian outcome and random effects for dependence or
heterogeneity among clusters. They are useful for binary, count, proportion, and
other outcomes measured repeatedly within donors, animals, sites, families, or
experimental blocks.

For observation $j$ in cluster $i$, a GLMM specifies

$$
\boxed{
Y_{ij}\mid\mathbf b_i\sim\mathcal F(\mu_{ij},\phi),
\qquad
g(\mu_{ij})=\mathbf x_{ij}^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta
+\mathbf z_{ij}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf b_i,
\qquad
\mathbf b_i\sim N(\mathbf0,\mathbf G).
}
$$

Here $\mathcal F$ supplies the conditional outcome distribution, $g$ is a link,
$\boldsymbol\beta$ contains population coefficients, and $\mathbf b_i$ contains
latent cluster-specific deviations. Outcomes are commonly assumed independent
**conditional on** $\mathbf b_i$. They are dependent marginally because they
share the same latent effects.

A GLMM is therefore a full data-generating model, not simply a GLM with a
cluster indicator or a device for changing standard errors. The outcome family,
link, fixed effects, random-effects distribution, and sampling hierarchy all
contribute to its meaning.

# Start with the Target and the Experimental Unit

Suppose cells are sampled from donors and a binary outcome records whether each
cell expresses a marker. Cells are observational units, but donors are the
independently sampled biological units for a population claim about people. A
donor random intercept can describe residual donor heterogeneity and the
dependence among cells from the same donor. Thousands of cells do not turn ten
donors into thousands of biological replicates.

Different targets require different summaries:

| Scientific target | GLMM quantity | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Association within a latent cluster state | fixed coefficient $\beta_k$ | conditional link-scale contrast |
| Mean response in the population | $E_{\mathbf b}\{g^{-1}(\mathbf x^T\boldsymbol\beta+\mathbf z^T\mathbf b)\}$ | random-effect-averaged mean |
| Heterogeneity among clusters | component of $\mathbf G$ | latent between-cluster variation |
| Prediction for a sampled cluster | conditional prediction using $\widehat{\mathbf b}_i$ | cluster-specific fitted response |
| Prediction for a new cluster | predictive distribution integrating over a new $\mathbf b$ | new-cluster uncertainty |

The **estimand** is one of these population quantities. Maximum likelihood or a
Bayesian procedure supplies an **estimator**; the fitted number is an
**estimate**. These targets are not interchangeable.

# Conditional and Marginal Effects Differ

Consider a logistic random-intercept model,

$$
\operatorname{logit}\{P(Y_{ij}=1\mid b_i,x_{ij})\}
=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{ij}+b_i,
\qquad b_i\sim N(0,\tau^2).
$$

$\exp(\beta_1)$ is a conditional odds ratio comparing predictor values at the
same value of the latent intercept. The population-average probability is

$$
P(Y_{ij}=1\mid x_{ij})=
\int \operatorname{logit}^{-1}
(\beta_0+\beta_1x_{ij}+b)\,\varphi(b;0,\tau^2)\,db.
$$

The inverse link is nonlinear, so this integral is not generally
$\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\beta_0+\beta_1x)$. Consequently, the marginal odds
ratio is not simply $\exp(\beta_1)$ and usually moves toward one relative to its
conditional counterpart. This is a scale and averaging issue, not evidence that
one fit is wrong. Report the estimand and compute fitted probabilities or
standardized contrasts on the scale relevant to the scientific question.

With a log link and a normally distributed random intercept,

$$
E(Y_{ij}\mid x_{ij})
=\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1x_{ij})E\{\exp(b_i)\}
=\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1x_{ij}+\tau^2/2).
$$

In this special case, integrating over the intercept changes the mean level but
preserves the multiplicative contrast $\exp(\beta_1)$. Random slopes or more
complex covariance structures can remove that simplification.

# Dependence, Overdispersion, and Random Slopes

A random intercept induces association among outcomes in the same cluster. A
random slope additionally lets the cluster response to time, treatment, or dose
vary. For example,

$$
g(\mu_{ij})=\beta_0+\beta_1t_{ij}+b_{0i}+b_{1i}t_{ij},
\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}b_{0i}\\b_{1i}\end{pmatrix}
\sim N\!\left(\mathbf0,
\begin{pmatrix}\tau_0^2&\tau_{01}\\\tau_{01}&\tau_1^2\end{pmatrix}\right).
$$

This model produces both heterogeneous trajectories and a time-dependent
within-cluster association. Centering time changes the meaning of the intercept
and intercept--slope covariance. The design must include enough clusters and
enough within-cluster time variation to identify the random slope.

Random effects can also create extra-Poisson or extra-binomial variation, but
not every form of overdispersion is cluster heterogeneity. Zero inflation,
unmodeled exposure, serial dependence, omitted predictors, and a wrong
mean--variance relationship are different mechanisms. A cluster random effect
should represent a plausible sampling level rather than serve as an automatic
repair for a large residual statistic.

# Marginal Likelihood and Its Approximations

Conditional on $\mathbf b_i$, cluster $i$ contributes

$$
L_i(\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf G,\phi\mid\mathbf b_i)
=\prod_{j=1}^{n_i}f(y_{ij}\mid\mathbf b_i).
$$

The observed-data likelihood integrates out the latent effect:

$$
\boxed{
L(\boldsymbol\beta,\mathbf G,\phi)
=\prod_{i=1}^{m}
\int
\left\{\prod_{j=1}^{n_i}f(y_{ij}\mid\mathbf b_i)\right\}
\varphi(\mathbf b_i;\mathbf0,\mathbf G)\,d\mathbf b_i.
}
$$

Unlike the Gaussian linear mixed model, this integral rarely has a closed form.
Common computational strategies include:

- a Laplace approximation, often accurate when clusters are informative and
  the latent dimension is modest;
- adaptive Gaussian quadrature, which can improve accuracy for low-dimensional
  random effects at greater computational cost;
- penalized quasi-likelihood, historically important but potentially biased for
  binary data with small clusters or extreme probabilities; and
- Bayesian sampling or approximation, which replaces optimization of the
  marginal likelihood with posterior computation and makes prior sensitivity
  part of the analysis.

Agreement across optimizers does not establish that an approximation is
accurate. When the scientific conclusion is delicate, compare integration
settings or computational methods, inspect convergence diagnostics, and report
the software, parameterization, and approximation used.

# Estimation, Uncertainty, and Prediction

Maximum likelihood estimates $\boldsymbol\beta$ and the parameters of
$\mathbf G$ and $\phi$. Wald standard errors use local curvature of the
approximated log-likelihood. Profile likelihood or a cluster-level parametric
bootstrap can better represent skewness and boundary behavior, provided the
simulation reproduces the fitted hierarchy and the resampling target.

Testing a variance component against zero is nonregular because zero lies on
the boundary and some nuisance parameters may be unidentified under the null.
A routine chi-squared likelihood-ratio reference can therefore be wrong.
Prespecified bootstrap calibration, appropriate mixture references in simple
cases, or Bayesian posterior summaries are more defensible than an automatic
one-degree-of-freedom test.

The fitted $\widehat{\mathbf b}_i$ are shrunken conditional predictions, not
observed cluster traits. Their shrinkage depends on cluster size, information,
and $\widehat{\mathbf G}$. Treating them as error-free outcomes in a second
analysis discards prediction uncertainty. Prediction for a new cluster must
also integrate over a new random effect rather than set it equal to a fitted
effect from an existing cluster.

# Diagnostics and Sensitivity

Classical raw residual plots are difficult for discrete GLMMs because residuals
are nonnormal and their distribution changes with the fitted mean. Model
criticism should combine design checks, simulation, and targeted refits.

| Question | Evidence | Sensitivity or response |
|---|---|---|
| Is the mean structure adequate? | residual or predictive patterns by predictor, time, and cluster | add justified nonlinearities or interactions |
| Is the outcome distribution adequate? | zero frequencies, tails, dispersion, simulated envelopes | compare mechanism-specific families or observation models |
| Is dependence represented? | residual association within donor, time, batch, family, or site | revise random effects or serial correlation structure |
| Are random effects supported? | near-zero variances, correlations near $\pm1$, flat profiles | check design and scaling; report simpler-model sensitivity |
| Is integration accurate? | changes across quadrature points, approximation, optimizer, or starts | increase accuracy and compare computational methods |
| Are clusters influential? | leave-one-cluster-out changes and extreme conditional predictions | verify records and report influence sensitivity |
| Does the assumed random-effects distribution matter? | predictive mismatch or conclusion driven by few clusters | compare plausible distributions or robust formulations |

Simulation-based randomized quantile residuals can reveal distributional
misfit, but they cannot diagnose confounding, an incorrectly defined
experimental unit, informative cluster size, or missing-not-at-random outcomes.
Those problems require design knowledge and explicit sensitivity models.

# Bioinformatics Example: Cell-level Marker Detection

Suppose 30 donors are randomized to two ex vivo stimulation conditions, and
hundreds of cells are profiled from each donor. Let $Y_{ij}$ indicate marker
detection in cell $j$ from donor $i$. One possible model is

$$
Y_{ij}\mid b_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_{ij}),
\qquad
\operatorname{logit}(p_{ij})
=\beta_0+\beta_1A_i+\boldsymbol\gamma^{\mathsf T}\mathbf q_{ij}+b_i,
\qquad
b_i\sim N(0,\tau^2),
$$

where $A_i$ is condition and $\mathbf q_{ij}$ contains prespecified cell-level
quality variables. The donor is the experimental unit for the treatment
contrast; cells and sequencing reads are technical or subsampling levels.
Information about $\beta_1$ depends strongly on the 30 donors and allocation,
not merely the total cell count.

Statistically, $\exp(\beta_1)$ is a donor-conditional odds ratio under the
specified model. A population-average risk difference requires integration over
the random effects and standardization over a stated covariate distribution.
Biologically, either contrast describes marker detection, not necessarily true
expression or a molecular mechanism. Detection limits, cell-type composition,
doublets, donor selection, and batch--condition balance remain important.

A cell-level GLMM is also not automatically preferable to donor-level
aggregation. Pseudobulk or donor-level summaries can align the analysis more
directly with randomization and may be more robust when the cell-level
observation model is doubtful. Compare conclusions at the biological-unit level
and make the estimand explicit.

- [Generalized linear models](../regression-models/generalized-linear-models.qmd)
  supplies the outcome family, link, and conditional mean.
- [Link functions and exponential-family distributions](../regression-models/link-functions-and-exponential-family-distributions.qmd)
  explains the link and variance function.
- [Random intercepts and random slopes](random-intercepts-and-random-slopes.qmd)
  develops latent heterogeneity and design-supported covariance structures.
- [Linear mixed-effects models](linear-mixed-effects-models.qmd) gives the
  Gaussian special case, where marginal likelihood is more tractable.
- [Repeated measures and longitudinal data](repeated-measures-and-longitudinal-data.qmd)
  compares mixed models with marginal approaches for time-indexed data.
- [Parametric bootstrap](../statistical-inference/parametric-bootstrap.qmd) and
  [when asymptotic approximations fail](../asymptotic-thinking/when-asymptotic-approximations-fail.qmd)
  explain calibration and nonregular inference.

1. A GLMM is a conditional outcome model plus a probability model for latent
   group effects.
2. With nonlinear links, conditional coefficients and population-average
   effects are different estimands.
3. Likelihood evaluation requires integration, so approximation and computation
   are part of the inferential method.
4. Random effects must follow the design; they do not automatically cure
   overdispersion, confounding, or pseudoreplication.
5. Bioinformatics inference is primarily limited by independent biological
   units, even when each unit yields many cells or reads.
